visible.summary:
Slovenia is among Central and Eastern Europe's most progressive destinations for trans visitors, with a cleaner documented profile than its neighbours. Legal gender recognition is depathologised (no surgery or psychiatric-diagnosis requirement), and a 2022 reform abolished local jurisdiction in the gender-change procedure — reducing involuntary outing through local bureaucracy. Comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers gender identity, same-sex marriage is legal (2022, via the Constitutional Court), and no far-right party is in government.

No severe traveler-axis incidents surfaced in research: no mob violence against trans people, no trans-tourist rape, no European Court case of police abuse, and no documented foreign-trans-detention case — unlike several neighbours (Greece's Thessaloniki mob, Italy's tourist-rape and Milan police beating, Czechia's trans-foreigner extradition mishandling, Poland's foreign-trans-woman-in-male-detention). The main caveats are a far-right youth campaign ("Two Sexes, One Truth"), an underreporting/trust gap in hate-crime reporting, and thinner detention-placement evidence for a small country.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage legal since 2022 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The depathologised LGR regime and the 2022 local-jurisdiction reform are resident-facing administrative law.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is very low.

sources.claim: Country overview updated 12 Mar 2026: Slovenia is regarded as among the most progressive countries in Central and Eastern Europe on LGBTIQ rights - same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI organisations registerable - with comprehensive antidiscrimination laws enacted since 2016 explicitly covering sexual orientation and gender identity.
thin: no usable finding

Ministry of the Interior notice of 29 October 2022: the local-jurisdiction step in legal gender-change procedures was abolished on the recommendation of the Advocate of the Principle of Equality, so transgender persons are no longer exposed to involuntary disclosure of transgender identity in their local environment.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): Legebitra documented 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and TransAkcija documented 25 cases of direct bias-motivated incidents in 2023. After Pride, LGBTIQ+ organisations held a press conference about attacks and rising hate while the Prime Minister took three days to react and the Interior Minister made no statements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the Health Ministry officially confirmed to the Interdisciplinary Council for Gender Recognition that medical treatment is not required for legal gender recognition and formally asked the Interior Ministry to amend the relevant Civil Registry Act sub-article. The review also notes the death at 73 of a founder of Slovenia's grassroots LGBTI movement.

US State Department 2023 report on Slovenia: no laws criminalise consensual same-sex conduct and there were no reports of state-condoned violence, but authorities recorded violence incidents without tracking case numbers and local NGOs called violence against LGBTQI+ persons prevalent and under-reported. In June 2023 a woman wearing a rainbow flag was assaulted near the Ljubljana Pride route, marchers had eggs thrown at them and rainbow flags were burned on video.

ENACT national report of January 2025 (EU CERV-2023 project): civil society provides LGBTI hate-crime victims counselling, advocacy and safe spaces, but LGBTI persons using generic victim-support services face heteronormative hurdles. The report documents institutional shortcomings in the anti-LGBTI hate-crime framework.

UPI report of 25 July 2006: Slovenia passed a law legalising same-sex marriage but restricted the ceremony to the two partners plus a local community registration official - no friends or relatives. Gay and lesbian organisations welcomed the move as a concrete step while criticising the law as 'insufficient'.

Inquirer/AFP (Dec 2015): Pope Francis urged Slovenian politicians to 'support the family' four days before the referendum on the gay-marriage law adopted by parliament in March - the referendum (later lost) followed a conservative challenge.

visible.summary:
Estonia is broadly workable with a strong progressive trajectory but a social climate that lags the law. It was the first Baltic and post-Soviet country to legalise same-sex marriage (2024), approved a national LGBT+ equal-opportunities action plan in 2025 (with particular attention to trans people), joined 16 EU states in urging Hungary to revise its anti-LGBT laws, and held Tallinn Pride in 2025. There are no documented severe traveler-axis incidents — no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality, or foreign-trans-detention case.

The notable gap is legal gender recognition: it remains medical-gatekept (it requires a diagnosis and is "complicated, arbitrary"; a reform bill stalled), and surveys show Estonians are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (62% avoid holding hands; 40% avoid certain locations for fear of assault).

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage legal since 2024 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The medical-gatekept LGR regime and its stalled reform bill are resident-facing.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime very low.

sources.claim: ERR News: Estonia approved a national LGBT+ equal-opportunities action plan (approved by Economy Minister Erkki Keldo, developed over ~2 years by the Equality Policies Department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications; photo-dated Tallinn Pride 31 May 2025). Sets targets across education (inclusive curricula, physical/mental safety of LGBTIQ students and staff), healthcare, employment and legal-framework reform, anchored on 'Estonia should be a great place for LGBTIQ people to live'. Trans-relevant: legal framework to be updated to support gender identity/expression protections.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): all same-sex relations legal nationwide; Estonia became the first Baltic state with marriage equality in June 2023 (incl. joint adoption; opposition filed 700+ amendments to block it, failed). Public support for marriage equality 53% (75% among 20-somethings) in 2023 vs 34% in 2012. National LGBTI equal-opportunities action plan approved 2025 with special attention to trans wellbeing; advocacy continues for self-determination-based legal gender recognition and hate-speech/hate-crime laws. LGBTI orgs can register.

Equaldex data for Estonia: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, no censorship; legal gender change legal but requires medical diagnosis; no nonbinary recognition; no hate-crime protections; employment discrimination prohibited on SOGI; housing discrimination protections cover sexual orientation only; conversion therapy not banned; bathroom access protected. Estonians rank #1 of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

F&M Global Barometer of Transgender Rights time series for Estonia (2011-2024): legal gender recognition exists but requires physiological alteration and psychiatric diagnosis; hate speech/crime legislation does not include gender identity; workplace/housing/healthcare anti-discrimination laws include gender identity; no known murders of gender-identity minorities.

TGEU/ILGA-Europe compliance report (2018) on Estonia's implementation of CoE Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5: covers hate crimes and data collection, safety of LGBT people deprived of liberty, hate speech, association, expression, transgender-specific health and private-life issues, employment, education, housing, sports and asylum.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Estonia: joined 16 EU states urging Hungary to revise its anti-LGBTI laws; Foreign Minister publicly supported Tallinn Pride and missions flew rainbow flags; in December Estonia adopted a national action plan to strengthen LGBTI equality across education, healthcare, employment and the legal system.

EU FRA LGBTIQ survey III country sheet for Estonia (2024): 62% avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (EU-27: 53%); 40% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (EU-27: 29%); 38% are open about being LGBTIQ (EU-27: 51%); work discrimination below EU average (12% vs 19%).

Estonian World (7 Jul 2017): foreign embassies and international missions in Tallinn issued a joint declaration for Baltic Pride 2017 (Tallinn, 6-9 July), affirming LGBTI rights as human rights and calling for an environment free from discrimination — external diplomatic backing for open LGBTI life in Estonia at a Pride moment.

LGBT Estonia (9 Oct 2021, Estonian): 7-year retrospective on the 2014 cohabitation act — implementation gaps forced litigation: a 2016 appeal court ordered Harju County Government to register an Estonian-Swedish same-sex marriage concluded in Sweden, and courts repeatedly found unequal treatment unconstitutional; the half-law era ended when marriage equality passed in 2023.

visible.summary:
Taiwan is a progressive Asian destination — it was the first in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage (2019), the government is investing US$8.76 million to double gender-neutral public bathrooms by 2029, and a trans march in Taipei drew 3,000 participants in 2025. There are no documented severe incidents (no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, or organised dating-app predation).

The main gaps are legal-gender-recognition reform stagnation — a 2008 Ministry order still requires sex-reassignment surgery to change one's gender marker (blocking an estimated 90% of trans people, with only case-by-case court exceptions), and the government has been "floundering" on reform — and a rising anti-gender discourse movement that has produced online waves of hostility. A trans woman was outed during a police identity inspection (the Viva case), and Taipei has held a vigil for victims of anti-trans violence.

For a visitor, bathrooms are unrestricted (and being proactively expanded to gender-neutral), there is no criminalisation, and border/immigration poses no trans-specific friction. Taipei City has trans-friendly service guidelines.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage legal since 2019 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The 2008 surgery-required gender-marker order and the stalled reform are resident-facing; the Viva outing case concerned a resident.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; earthquake/typhoon risks affect all travellers.

sources.claim: Taiwan Insight (Feb 2026): 'What about trans rights? Taiwan's ongoing struggle for self-ID' - the 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery to change legal gender blocks an estimated 90% of trans people from obtaining matching national ID; every ID-requiring aspect of daily life (clinics, airport security) becomes a potential site of distress and discrimination; the Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013.

Taiwan Insight (Jan 2026): the Taiwanese government continues to flounder on transgender rights in 2025 amidst continued transphobia - no tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction; pending conscription-criteria changes could actively harm trans people; anti-gender movement activity rising, with organisations supporting Trump's anti-trans policies and the Taiwan Solidarity Party calling for a 'two genders' position.

Taipei Times (Aug 2024): the Ministry of Environment will invest NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms nationwide (623 to 1,246 by 2029); of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents reporting discrimination, 17% occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms.

Focus Taiwan (Nov 2025): 'Most Taiwan all-gender restrooms do not meet standards: Rights group' — an LGBTQ+ rights group finds only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying page addressed Taiwan's transgender rights - laws, protections and gaps.
New Bloom (Nov 2024): analysis of the wave of anti-gender discourse in Taiwan - rising anti-gender movement activity and its political context.

TaiwanPlus (Aug 2024): a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change the gender marker on her government ID without requiring surgery or a psychological evaluation; the supporting rights group says they will likely appeal.

JURIST dispatch (Nov 2025): the 7th annual Taiwan Transgender March in Taipei drew an estimated 3,000 people despite rain, with international participants; calls for an end to discrimination against trans people as the rights debate continues.

Utopia Asia Taiwan travel and resources page: 'one of Asia's most progressive countries for LGBT rights, and certainly the most liberal of the Chinese diaspora'; notes Taiwan regularised adoption for same-sex parents on May 16, 2023; listings of organisations, bars, spas and venues across 12 cities.

visible.summary:
Malaysia is dangerous — one of the few countries that criminalises gender expression per se. All 13 states and the Federal Territory prohibit "a man posing as a woman" under Sharia law (up to 3 years in jail, a fine, and caning). While these laws technically apply to Muslims, the enforcement climate affects all trans people: religious police conduct systematic raids on trans events — tipping off media in advance and sharing detainees' faces with tabloids (public outing and humiliation). Three trans women were killed in fewer than two months in 2019.

The political climate is shifting toward Islamist parties (a deputy minister urged the "deviant culture" label for LGBTQ; state-backed "rehabilitation" programs; dating-site blocking). For a non-Muslim foreign trans visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing law doesn't directly apply, but being caught in a raided venue, facing the enforcement climate, or being subject to Section 377A (same-sex conduct, 20 years + whipping, applies to all including tourists) are real risks. There is no legal gender recognition.
visible.tangentialFactors: Section 377A (same-sex conduct, 20 years + whipping) applies to all including tourists — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General crime and Islamic-law compliance (alcohol, dress codes for religious sites) affect Muslim and non-Muslim travellers in different ways; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust country profile — Malaysia (live page in cache): federal Penal Code section 377 criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 20 years plus whipping), alongside Sharia enactments across the states prohibiting 'cross-dressing' or 'males posing as females' — including the Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 covering 'sodomy' and 'sexual intercourse against the order of nature'. Situates Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise, with active litigation listed alongside the Mauritius and Namibia cases.

Human Rights Watch report (10 August 2022) 'I Don't Want to Change Myself', based on interviews with 73 LGBT people in Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 across seven states plus journalists and lawyers: every state and the federal territories (Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya) maintain Sharia codes criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity ('a man posing as a woman'), while the federal penal code punishes oral/anal sex with up to 20 years plus mandatory whipping. Government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events/media content were censored. The 2021 Nur Sajat case shows enforcement reach — 122 religious officers were mobilised to hunt her over 'insulting Islam' before she fled to Thailand and gained UNHCR protection.

Human Rights Watch (25 June 2019): a transgender woman was killed in Klang, a Kuala Lumpur suburb — the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months — with the piece documenting violence against trans people alongside police mistreatment and impunity ('The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself').
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Aug 2023) covers growing LGBTQ fears in Malaysia as Islamists shatter reform hopes.

The Diplomat (10 December 2025): on 28 November police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B — the largest such raid since 2022 — with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked, suspending 17 civil servants identified among them. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet release was delayed; over 130 remained held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang. Documents current enforcement-and-exposure risks against queer spaces, including for foreign visitors.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (DNS failure); the underlying Human Rights Law Centre case summary covers the Malaysian High Court denying a request to declare Sharia law prohibiting cross-dressing unconstitutional.
NOTE: The UNDP/Asia Pacific Transgender Network publication on Malaysia returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

International Commission of Jurists (July 2020): Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Mohamad Al-Bakri announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) 'full licence to carry out its enforcement actions' against transgender persons; the ICJ condemned the order, demanded its revocation and called for non-discrimination guarantees. Documents state-sanctioned targeting of trans people in the federal territories.

Malaysia4U legal guide (updated July 2026): sections 377A/377B criminalise 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' for any person regardless of gender or consent — maximum 20 years plus whipping — and apply to tourists; state Syariah offences (liwat, musahaqah, cross-dressing) apply only to Muslims (max 3 years, RM5,000 fine, 6 strokes). The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Syariah provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds without decriminalising anything under the Penal Code; enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted. No same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law; sodomy first criminalised in 1871.

Human Rights Watch (24 September 2014) 'I'm Scared to Be a Woman': since the 1980s every one of Malaysia's 13 states has passed Sharia enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people — all 13 bar Muslim men from 'dressing as women' and three also bar 'women posing as men' — enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. Documents the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of Victoria by religious officials, repeated arrests (one woman over 20 times), routine rejection of gender-marker changes by the Registration Department (a 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery), and prison terms of four months to three years with male-ward sexual violence. Follows the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014 that triggered the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge (Court of Appeal decision then expected 7 November 2014).

visible.summary:
Singapore is broadly workable — far safer than its neighbour Malaysia, with no criminalisation of trans identity, no religious police, and one of the world's lowest crime rates. Section 377A (which criminalised sex between men) was repealed in 2022, and the prison service reports no assaults against its 10 transgender inmates — unusually positive for axis-H. Singapore is also a regional medical hub with gender-affirming care available.

The main gaps: legal gender recognition requires genital surgery (expensive and restrictive), there is no anti-discrimination law (the 2025 Workplace Fairness Act explicitly excludes sexual orientation and gender identity), and over 65% of trans Singaporeans report negative workplace experiences. A radio code still groups homosexuality with "paedophilia and incest" as lifestyles barred from the airwaves. Progress has "stalled" since the 377A repeal, with discrimination "quietly tolerated."

For a visitor: efficient border processing, very low street crime, unrestricted bathrooms, and no trans-specific police friction. The atmosphere is conservative but quietly accommodating in practice.
visible.tangentialFactors: The radio code grouping homosexuality with "paedophilia and incest" is a climate signal; the 2022 repeal of 377A removed partner-related criminal exposure for visitors.
visible.localsOnly: The surgery-required LGR regime, the Workplace Fairness Act exclusion, and the 65% negative-workplace-experience figure are resident-facing; the prison-service data concerns resident inmates.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General crime is extremely low; no trans-specific travel advisory.

sources.claim: MPSC report (Feb 2025): transgender community faces several key challenges to health and well-being. These include (1) the difficult process of legal gender recognition, which has a prohibitive cost due to the required genital surgeries; (2) discrimination, abuse and restrictions facing transgender students; (3) discrimination against transgender persons in the employment sector; (4) discrimination and harassment in healthcare settings that discourag

Outright International Singapore overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal for men and women; legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations cannot register — registration remains the structural gap despite decriminalisation.

Straits Times (15 Nov 2023): the Singapore Prison Service reported 10 transgender inmates currently behind bars and no recorded cases of assault against transgender inmates — a rare official datum on trans prisoners in the system.

Pink Dot SG (8 Jan 2025): the new Workplace Fairness Legislation gives Singapore its first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but it stops short of covering LGBTQ+ workers — gender identity/expression are not protected grounds, leaving workplace exposure for trans staff.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature (June 2023) covers Singapore's LGBT community feeling safer as the end of the 377A ban brings change.

South China Morning Post (3 Jul 2025): a clause of the radio broadcast code grouping homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden 'lifestyles' sparked calls for review — a former radio DJ and actor argued the grouping 'has no place in a post-377A Singapore'. Media-regulation residue after decriminalisation.

F&M Global Barometers Singapore country profile: interactive scores across unified/gay/transgender rights indices and an LGBTQI+ perception index, 2011–2024, covering de jure protections and lived experience — score values are served dynamically and are not extractable from the fetched text.

Intrepid Travel 'Is Singapore LGBTQIA+ friendly': describes a thriving LGBTQIA+ social scene — gay-friendly bars (e.g. Backstage Bar in Chinatown), pop-ups and exhibitions — alongside practical guidance on solo travel and room sharing for its own trips. Visitor-facing operator guidance.

visible.summary:
Iran is one of the world's most severe environments for trans people — but with a unique bifurcation. Same-sex conduct carries the death penalty, and a trans woman was raped in Ministry of Intelligence custody (the documented case of Ghazal Marzban in Evin Prison, 2023). The Tehran City Council ordered trans people to avoid "busy" areas of the capital. Trans people who have not had surgery face immorality and indecency provisions (imprisonment, fines, lashes) and documented forced-transition pressure — 6Rang describes "40 years of forcing gay people to choose between transitioning and death."

However, transsexuality IS legally recognised in Iran (under a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini), and gender-affirming surgery is state-funded — making Iran one of the few countries in the region with any legal recognition of trans identity, and a trans medical-tourism hub. A post-operative trans visitor with matching documents is in a structurally different and better position than a pre-operative or non-binary visitor, or anyone perceived as same-sex-active — who face the death penalty, state-custody sexual violence, and forced-transition coercion.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct carries the death penalty — a catastrophic risk for any visitor perceived as same-sex-active, including trans people whose documents don't match their presentation or relationships.
visible.localsOnly: The 1987 fatwa's legal recognition of transsexuality and state-funded gender-affirming surgery are resident-facing; the forced-transition pressure on gay people is a resident phenomenon, though it signals the state's posture.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General state-surveillance risks, compulsory hijab for all women, and the risk of arbitrary detention for foreign nationals affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: RFE/RL: Tehran authorities publicly warned transgender people to avoid 'busy' areas — official advisories restricting trans visibility in public space, illustrating state pressure on gender-nonconforming people in Iran.
HRANA: imprisoned trans rights activist Ghazal Marzban's open letter recounts rape in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility — documented custodial violence against trans detainees.

6Rang submission (Feb 2025) to the UN Independent Expert on SOGI, 'They See Us as Criminals: The Forces Driving LGBTIQ+ Displacement from Iran': survey of 25 LGBTIQ+ people who fled Iran (96% from ethnic minorities) documenting systematic persecution driving displacement.
Outright International country overview: Iran at-a-glance — same-sex relations illegal nationwide for men and women, with the policy/legal-status matrix as baseline reference.

UK Home Office CPIN Iran: Sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v5.0, Dec 2025): the Islamic Penal Code criminalises all same-sex activity (flogging to death penalty); no discrimination protections; convictions on pretext of more severe charges; gender reassignment surgery is permitted and may be subsidised after a 'gender identity disorder' diagnosis, but is invasive and often sub-standard; recognition only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process; an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution.

LGBTQ Nation (2025): trans medical tourism booming in Iran while transitions are forced on locals — foreign patients seek state-subsidised surgery while Iranian trans people face pressure to conform to binary transition or face legal penalty.

Business Insider: the state funds gender-reassignment surgery but the price is dignity — analysis of how Iran's conditional tolerance coerces trans Iranians (surgical pressure framed as 'protection').

6Rang submission to Iran's UPR (48th session, Jan-Feb 2025): human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people in Iran - documentation of persecution, violence and legal discrimination.
Human Rights Watch (21 Nov 2005): two more men executed for homosexual conduct in Iran — recorded state execution practice for same-sex conduct, the enforcement backdrop for trans/LGBT visitors.
